data.content_ref: inline:The mechanism section concludes with 'It follows that the underlying structure was never relevant to the outcome at all,' presented as a deductive consequence ('It follows that…') of the preceding argument. This is a non sequitur that also directly contradicts the claim's own central concept. The entire claim is built on 'verisimilitude' (truth-likeness): preferring better-corroborated theories is supposedly a methodological rule to 'maximize verisimilitude.' But verisimilitude is a relational property between a theory and the actual structure of reality — it presupposes that the underlying structure of the truth is precisely what makes one theory better than another. If that underlying structure is 'never relevant to the outcome,' then verisimilitude is vacuous: there is no truth to be close to, and the preference lacks any coherent target. This is exactly the scenario the target's own first countercondition warns about ('the preference lacks a coherent target' if verisimilitude cannot be consistently defined). The target thus internally self-destructs: the mechanism's final entailment negates the very telos the claim needs the preference to have. Nothing in the preceding sentences (asymmetry of falsification, corroboration as past-test severity, 'best bet' formulation) entails irrelevance of underlying structure; if anything they presuppose it, since 'surviving tests that would have killed a false one' only matters if there is a true structure that false theories fail to match.
